text: Welcome to week 10 of the official
NASCAR Gen 4 Cup Series. And this week,
you'll be taking on the Michigan
International Speedway for 60 laps. For
qualifying, you probably know the drill.
Use your warm-up and first time laps to
get some heat in your tires in
preparation for your final lap. And take
this time to get familiar with the
bottom line in turns one and two. You'll
notice that it has slightly less
banking. And while I would usually tell
you to avoid running on the flatter
pavement, running a shorter distance in
that side of the track could be the
difference between starting first and
11th this week. Continue running around
the track through your first time lap
until you hit turns three and four. Run
the car up the track and give yourself
as much momentum as you can to take the
white flag. Shorten your route to the
finish line, but don't use the apron
just yet.
[Music]
Once you hit the line, let the car
wander up the track to the outside wall
and stay there until you reach the
caution light. Drive the car into the
corner and lift off the gas. Drag the
brakes to get the nose pointed onto the
flatter pavement and ease back onto the
throttle as you feel the car stick. As
soon as you can feel the car fully
settle, put your foot to the floor and
ride the right sides out of the corner.
The wall comes up quickly if you mess
this up, so you'll need to be decisive
on the throttle. Heading into turn
three, start turning down the track just
before the black banner on the wall.
Lift, drag the brakes, aim for the white
line, and try to carry as much speed as
you can around the shortest distance you
can muster. Let the car track out as far
as it wants before you aim it back down
the track, straightening your run to the
finish line.

Once you take the green flag, you'll be
rolling onto the throttle in second
gear. Wheel spin shouldn't be too bad
this week, but as the race goes on, it
will become more difficult to get the
power down, so be wary of that as the
tires wear. Unfortunately, you're in for
another week of draft racing. So, once
you find an opening against the wall in
the straightaways, take it. I ran 10
laps around the top and bottom grooves
at a comfortable pace. And as expected,
the outside provided the most wear on
the right front, trending tighter as the
run went on. With that in mind, the
outside is the only lane where you'll be
able to guarantee that draft on the
backstretch. So, if you need to bite the
bullet and add weight to the load on
your right front to stay in line, it's a
sacrifice worth making. In the case that
you find yourself out of traffic, the
inside will be your better choice. But
as we mentioned earlier, the flatter
portion of banking in the corners is not
the place to go unless you find yourself
with a massive run in a light race
restart. It gets tight down there and it
opens you up to the possibility of a car
on your outside pinching you and forcing
you to lift. So, if you're going to run
the inside, use the first seam as the
reference point for where you want to
plant your left front tire. That alone
will give you the pivot you need to even
out the wear on your right sides. Facing
a fuel window of 36 to 40 laps, it goes
without saying that a fuel stop will be
guaranteed regardless of the number of
cautions. As far as tire strategy is
concerned, taking the unbeaten path
could be your key to coming out on top
this week. But it depends on how well
you treat your tires and how the
handling evolves before your first stop.
If the race runs green, I would advise
to take all four. But if you find
yourself halfway through what would be a
full tire run, consider giving right
sides only a shot. Taking two tires
offers the weaknesses you would expect
on the long run, but you can compensate
for it through the draft. This was the
end of a 45lap run to the finish in a
55lap race. I took right sides only on
my great flag pit stop. While I got
passed by the eventual winner, the draft
kept me with them until the end. The
only thing keeping me from making the
winning pass was the wear that I had to
put on my right side tires to compensate
for skipping the left sides. If I can do
this on 20 lap older left side tires,
it's fair to assume that you'd be able
to pull it off under a shorter run.
If you can avoid overd driving your
corners, hit your marks when it comes
time to pit, and avoid the incidents
that come with draft racing, you might
find yourself in a fantastic position as
the race unfolds. Good luck.
